# ECON 0100 | Homework C1 | Externalities

::: solution

# Solutions

:::

*Answers and work are shown in the red blocks.*

## Q1 | Malodorous Byproducts

Butterbeer is beloved by Hogwarts students and teachers alike and is widely available at wizarding shops. But the beverage has the negative effect of generating displeasing odors from its imbibers. Model the private market for butterbeer using private and social cost and benefit curves. Indicate on your graph the private equilibrium quantity and social equilibrium quantity.

Preferences for butterbeer and its marginal cost can be represented by the following relationships.

$$
D: P_B = 40 - Q_D \qquad\qquad S: P_S = 10 + \frac{1}{2} Q_S
$$

Prices are in galleons and quantity is in bottles. The odor imposes a cost of 9 galleons per bottle on everyone nearby.

Marginal Social Cost: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

Market Equilibrium Price: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ Market Equilibrium Quantity: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

Socially Efficient Quantity: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ Deadweight Loss: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

::::: solution

Marginal Social Cost: $P = 19 + \frac{1}{2} Q$. Market Equilibrium Price: $20$ galleons. Market Equilibrium Quantity: $20$ bottles. Socially Efficient Quantity: $14$ bottles. Deadweight Loss: $27$ galleons.

:::: {.columns gutter=1em}

::: column

Demand is the marginal private benefit (MPB) and supply is the marginal private cost (MPC). The odor adds $9$ of cost to every bottle, borne by people nearby, so the marginal social cost sits $9$ above supply:

$$
\text{MSC} = (10 + \tfrac{1}{2} Q) + 9 = 19 + \tfrac{1}{2} Q
$$

The market ignores the odor, so it clears where demand meets supply:

$$
40 - Q = 10 + \tfrac{1}{2} Q \quad\Rightarrow\quad Q = 20, \quad P = 20
$$

The efficient quantity counts the odor, so demand meets MSC:

$$
40 - Q = 19 + \tfrac{1}{2} Q \quad\Rightarrow\quad Q = 14, \quad P = 26
$$

:::

::: column

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,){width=100%}

:::

::::

Bottles $15$ through $20$ cost society more (MSC) than buyers value them (MPB), yet the market makes them. The deadweight loss is the triangle between MSC and demand over those $6$ bottles. Its height at $Q = 20$ is $\text{MSC} - \text{MPB} = 29 - 20 = 9$:

$$
\text{DWL} = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 9 \times (20 - 14) = 27
$$

:::::

## Q2 | Dragon Pox

Dragon Pox is spreading through the wizarding world. A dose of Gorsemoor’s Draught keeps a witch or wizard from catching it, so whoever drinks it also can’t pass Dragon Pox on to anyone else. Let’s model the market for the draught and assume the following.

1. There is a linear marginal private benefit curve for the draught.
2. The draught carries with it a positive externality.
3. There is a linear upward sloping supply curve for the draught. ~~The supply curve for the vaccine is a little funny, and we’ll talk about imperfect close substitutes in the next few weeks. But we’ll just assume it’s there.~~

Use a graph to discuss the welfare in the market and any potential market failure.

The graph below shows the market, with prices in galleons and quantity in doses. The upper downward-sloping curve is marginal social benefit and the lower one is marginal private benefit. Supply is both the private and the social cost. The lettered regions are for the questions.

![Market for Gorsemoor’s Draught with MPB, MSB and S, and regions A, B and C](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Market Quantity: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ Socially Efficient Quantity: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

Deadweight Loss region (letter): \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

::::: solution

Market Quantity: $10$ doses. Socially Efficient Quantity: $13$ doses. Deadweight Loss region: B.

:::: {.columns gutter=1em}

::: column

Buyers weigh only their own benefit, so the market clears where MPB meets supply. On the graph MPB is $P = 24 - Q$ and supply is $P = 4 + Q$:

$$
24 - Q = 4 + Q \quad\Rightarrow\quad Q = 10, \quad P = 14
$$

The efficient quantity counts the benefit to everyone else, so MSB, $P = 30 - Q$, meets supply:

$$
30 - Q = 4 + Q \quad\Rightarrow\quad Q = 13, \quad P = 17
$$

The doses from $10$ to $13$ are worth more to society (MSB) than they cost (S), but they never happen. The lost surplus is the triangle between MSB and supply over those units: region B, worth $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 6 \times 3 = 9$.

Region A is the external benefit the first $10$ doses already give to others; it is gained, not lost. Region C lies below supply, under cost, so it is not surplus at all.

:::

::: column

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,){width=100%}

:::

::::

:::::

Why does the market provide too few doses?

> a\) Each dose costs society more to brew than it costs the seller.
>
> b\) Each dose is worth more to society than to the witch or wizard buying it, so at the market quantity marginal social benefit is still above marginal cost.
>
> c\) Buyers value each dose less than sellers’ marginal cost, so too few buyers enter the market.
>
> d\) The market quantity is already socially efficient, so no doses are missing.

::: solution

**b)**

A witch or wizard who drinks the draught also keeps Dragon Pox from spreading to the people around them, but does not count that benefit when deciding. At the market quantity of $10$, MSB is $20$ while marginal cost is only $14$, so one more dose would add $6$ of surplus. a) describes an external cost, the butterbeer story, not this one. c) is wrong because at $Q = 10$ the buyer’s value equals marginal cost; buyers are not underpaying, they are leaving out others’ benefit. d) is wrong because the market stops $3$ short of the efficient $13$.

:::

## Q3 | Deadweight Loss Intuition

Which of the following best explains the intuition behind the deadweight loss associated with a negative externality like the one in Q1?

> a\) The externality causes the market to produce too much of the good, leading to a surplus and reduced consumer surplus.
>
> b\) The externality causes the market to produce too little of the good, leading to a shortage and reduced producer surplus.
>
> c\) The externality causes the market to produce at a quantity where the marginal social cost of production exceeds the marginal social benefit of consumption, leading to inefficiency and reduced total surplus.
>
> d\) The externality causes the market to produce at a quantity where the marginal social benefit of consumption exceeds the marginal social cost of production, leading to inefficiency and reduced total surplus.

::: solution

**c)**

The market ignores the odor, so it keeps making bottles past the efficient $14$, out to $20$. On each of those extra bottles the marginal social cost is above the marginal social benefit (in Q1 the odor has no external benefit, so MSB is demand), and the gap summed over them is the deadweight loss, a loss of total surplus. a) is wrong because the market still clears, with no surplus of unsold goods, and the loss is to total surplus, not only consumer surplus. b) has the direction backwards: a negative externality brings too much of the good, not too little. d) describes a positive externality, like Q2, where MSB stays above MSC at the market quantity.

:::

If the marginal cost of a gallon of gas is \$4.00, the negative externality is \$2.50, and the marginal benefit is \$4.50, what is the deadweight loss?

Deadweight Loss: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

::: solution

Deadweight Loss: \$2.00.

The buyer values the gallon at \$4.50 and it costs the seller \$4.00, so they trade it. But it also costs everyone else \$2.50, so its marginal social cost is $4.00 + 2.50 = 6.50$, more than its \$4.50 benefit. Selling it leaves society $6.50 - 4.50 = 2.00$ worse off; that \$2.00 is the deadweight loss. This is the choice above for one trade: the market makes it because the buyer’s benefit covers the seller’s cost, and society loses on it once the external cost is counted.

:::
